newsitem.title: USA: U.S. July jobs rise seen tamer, market grip fading.
newsitem.headline: U.S. July jobs rise seen tamer, market grip fading.

text.p: The relentless U.S. job machine probably churned out another healthy, though smaller, batch in July but bond investors nevertheless seem to be shedding their fixation on payrolls data, economists said.

While the employment figures, due at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT on Friday, have clearly not dropped off the radar screen, traders increasingly view them as irrelevant since the tighest labor markets in memory have generated barely a whiff of inflation.
"I don't think the market really cares so much about continued payrolls gains, which are pretty much in line with trend," said Astrid Adolfson, an economist with MCM MoneyWatch.
"For each of the employment reports its been a ho-hummer," she continued. "On the stronger ones, obviously the market dips but everyone takes them as a reason to buy and nothing more than that."
The Labor Department is expected to report that non-farm payrolls grew another 193,000 in July, compared with 217,000 in June, according to economists surveyed by Reuters.

Forecasters also expect, on average, the unemployment rate to dip back to 4.9 percent, where it stood in April. The jobless rate stood at 5.0 percent in June, up from May's 4.8 percent, its lowest level in over 20 years.

"There is not a lot of hysteria. If the unemployment rate started heading down towards 4.5 percent maybe that would be a different story," said James Glassman, senior economist at Chase Securities Inc.
"Everybody is kind of focused more on the labor cost side, the employment cost index (ECI) and wages part of this," Glassman continued.
But Tuesday's ECI numbers already confirmed companies have yet to feel a pinch from increased labor costs and so have no compelling need to pass along higher expenses to consumers.

Although total compensation, according to the ECI, rose 0.8 percent in the second quarter, following a 0.6 percent rise in the first, employers granted wage and salary increases at a less-generous 0.8 percent, compared to 0.9 percent.

Economists see average hourly earnings increasing just 0.2 percent in July, after a 0.3 percent rise in June. The consensus estimate for the average workweek is 34.6 hours, a bit shorter than June's 34.7 hours.
But the earnings component of the jobs report is hard to pin down and is not an entirely accurate indicator of wage inflation, they said.

"Since overtime costs a lot -- time and a half -- when companies boost overtime it tends to raise average hourly earnings. But of course companies like to do this because they don't have to hire," Glassman said.

The market believes that by shifting its unemployment rate forecasts for the remainder of 1997 down to 4.75 to 5.0 percent, the Federal Reserve this month signalled it can live with the current unemployment rate, economists said.

"If it comes in the way we forecast, it shouldn't mean anything," said Jay Feldman, analyst at Credit Suisse First Boston Corp, citing the firm's expectations of a 190,000 payrolls gain and a 4.9 percent jobless rate.
"I don't think the Fed is necessarily looking at some ... value in terms of the unemployment rate to tighten, because it's below 5.0 percent and they've forgone any action," he concluded.
